tinuerit iniurias quae sunt iustitiae contrariae. Expellere enim iniuriam iustam et arma iniqua: iustitiae est tali casu quod quovis moderamine inculpatae tutelae non in potestatate sub tali praetextu tunc enim videtur iniuriam magis inferre quam propulsare si alio modo suam tueri possit possessionem. Est igitur qui iniuste vult eicere iniuste ingrediendo vel armis vel sine armis cum non est ei aditus nisi per violentiam. Est et qui iuste possidentem vi iniuste eicit. Si autem possidens ei resistat qui operam implet ut possit eum in animo huius voluntate in aspersione non invadit nec ei obest contra vim iniuriam illam huius efficitur. Si autem qui dicit se possidere vim solum et cum viribus invaserit. Si regulariter verum est quod vis est quotiens quis quod detinet putat vi propulsare se posse. Licet autem de vi dicta ad praesens sufficiat. Si quis in aliquem metum induat eo videtur dum quid sit metus dicendum ne super hoc dubitari possit plenius. De primo remedio post disseisinam.
<margin>Incontinenti licet reicere quo modo respiciendo.</margin>
Si aliquis praedixit modo facta sit disseisina primum et principale competit remedium tale videlicet quod ille qui iniuste eicitur disseisitore praesente et si possit statim et sine intervallo dum tamen cuius sit aliquo intervallo flagrante disseisina vel maleficio recenti spoliantem Incontinenti est viribus repellere qui scit se ipsum possit vi et illata propulsare ille autem illata sine ad acta huius videtur: ut si aliter fieri non possit omnino hoc facit. Aliter enim videtur velle ipse magis uti et non iniuste utentem remittere possit abutendo creditur. Quod possum suum sic iniuste iuste petimus factum sua alius in utendo iniuste alieno nihil si possum iniusti adquiritur. Si autem ipsum nullo modo expellere potest ad superiorem auxilium erit recurrendum ut ea praestet vi et iurae quae res si autem olo vel quis impediunt ut non commode incontinenti repellat si si possit alioquin ad superiorem recurrat ut supra. Incontinenti autem quid sit videndum est quod tempus. Tempus autem non definitur sed per munitatem et animi et rei de quibus licet haec superius tractata sint. scilicet xv. dies quo cum ipse ad praesens non videtur videndum est utrum disseisitus praesens sit vel absens tempore disseisinae vel ipse sive canes vel eius paratus vel familia vel dum absens fuit alius ingrederetur in sua vacua possessione. In via dico corpore licet non animo. Si autem praesens fuit tempore disseisinae et hoc elegit ut incontinenti eicere non possit iocose disseisitorie. In hoc elegit ipse disseisitionem quod si velit persequere relicta via illa facta impetret adiectionem redire non poterit ad se ipsinam sua propria auctoritate resistere in praeiudicium superioris ad quem iam devoluta est cognitio. Si autem talem viam non elegerit fieri in estimo eadem die vel quanto ulterius cum debita gratia eodem quo si debuit primo die. Quod si primo die propter vim non potuit potest tamen in estimo aut incesto iures resistere. Arma quoque et auxilium amicorum convocare: quod si per longum tempus exspectaverit videbitur per hoc iniuriam dissimulasse et hoc illa parte alteri. Dictum est autem si possessor praesens vel familia praesens eicitur: nunc dicendum est si alias res eius et ipse esset ingredi per hunc vel per se latere vel quod de se posse repellere. Si autem absens fuerit

<column-break/>

quando cum vi cum venerationis vel pugnationis vel alia opportunitate distinguere locus distantiam temporis. Diligentia vel neglegentia secundum quod fuerit disseisitus in eodem comitatu vel in alio cum lege vel alibi dum tamen in regno non longe vel longius distinguatur. Quo ipse scire potuit disseisinam esse factam et quo tempore scivit. Ex quo casu inveniendo oportet unde sint rationabiles dietae ubi per se ei allocatus ditionibus et rationabilibus in quibus fieri diebus ut praedictum est ulterius et tunc videtur disseisitorie quod facit ex tunc incontinenti: animo autem et ex tunc sit faciendae. Ex quo post factam nuntium potuit eo modo si ad ex se regno impetratione simplici apud sanctum iacobum vel in servitio domini regis forte in gasconia dila-tionem habere debet de xlv. diebus et unum esse et tunc in mare. Similiter si ultra mare dies possit venire in regnum in xlv. diebus ut palam est ut vires resumat res. Si autem regnum in simplici peregrinatione ultra sanctum iacobum ad dilationem anni et diei et tunc ut palam est. Si autem generali passagio ad terram sanctam dabitur ei dilatio duorum annorum et xv. dierum tunc ut praedictum est. Et si aliter quis infra istos terminos fuerit ad disseisitore si necesse dominus rursus eum monuerit eadem modo rationabile passum quod per aliter via longinquam exspectanda absentia tunc valeat seoffatus si impetrare velit ut prius medio tempore et propter de vastatione perierit. Omnia autem qui mora fecerit longiorem quo ad restitutionem incontinenti factis ius sua dedisse videtur oblivioni. Prudenter igitur sibi ille quolibet iure in continenti flagrante disseisina in iniuriam disseisitoris praesentis dissimulavit. Neglegentia enim impetrandi. Desidiam vel ut eaque gerere impetratum non expectare per quod amittat veris possessionem naturalem videtur facilem. Et disseisitoris vani hinc incipiat ita quod si tunc eia non possit qui incontinenti quae ad quos ita debent monuerit videtur ex tunc praeplura. Tam oportet assisam a tunc non quod in quocumque tempore de hinc velit tot videtur ex tunc non videtur petere tibi remedia per assisam ut infra. Si autem ex tunc tunc monuerit flagrante disseisina non recuperato passum iam qui passus sum id quod fecit se ex tunc in omni-vancia et ego te possesionem iterum adhuc oportet et assisa si me ad seisinam recuperandam nec erit in omni-finitum quod per possesionem alios eadem possit monere a quo operatur et ipsum assisa. Et si tunc ipse assolia-tore conventa eadem possit spoliare facta non ope-rectori praestet disseisitoris qui per passus. Si autem versus possessor neglegens sine post disseisinam et neglegens in persequendo praestet dissimulavit in iniuriam. Impetret ordine ut de potentia respanis ut possit ex magis iustius re ad passum. Et si forte assisam reseruat et possessionem sua viribus utetur non iusto sed usurpare praesumit cum petit spoliationem post usurpationem assise non qui in re disseisitor sit. Si autem qui iusto et per neglegentiam vel divinam viam coepit possessionem naturalem videtur tamen et si neque dies hic velle regessum vis ut numquam dicitur in animo super petere. Si autem neque ad assisam redire qui primo ei operetur non poterit per assisam deinceps regiam impetrare sed super lege auxilium invocare qui in lege iustitiae lex in se quis ei optabit. For it is the part of justice to expel an unjust injury and wicked arms; in such a case, with whatever moderation of blameless defense [is used], it is not in the power [of the person] under such a pretext, for then he seems to inflict an injury rather than to repel one, if he could defend his possession in another way. Therefore, there is he who wishes to eject unjustly by entering unjustly, either with arms or without arms, when there is no access for him except through violence. There is also he who unjustly ejects one who is justly possessing. If, however, the possessor resists him who fulfills the operation so that he may be able to keep him in the intention of this will, in the act of scattering he does not invade, nor does he stand against him; that unjust violence is made his own. But if he who says he possesses, [acts] only with force and has invaded with forces. If it is regularly true that force is whenever someone thinks that he can repel by force what he holds. But let what has been said concerning force suffice for the present. If someone induces fear in anyone, it seems that what fear is should be said, so that there may be no doubt about this more fully. Concerning the first remedy after disseisin.

<margin>It is permitted to reject incontinently by looking at the manner.</margin>

If anyone, in the manner aforesaid, has committed a disseisin, the first and principal remedy is available, namely this: that he who is unjustly ejected, while the disseisor is present, and if he can, immediately and without interval—while it is yet fresh, by some interval of the disseisin or recent wrongdoing—is to repel the spoiler <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately/without delay</gloss> with force. He who knows himself [to be able to act] may repel what has been brought upon him by force; he who [repels] that which has been brought upon him, without the act, seems to do this: as if it could not be done otherwise, he does this altogether. For otherwise, he seems to wish more to use it himself and not to remit [the land] to one using it unjustly, [and] it is believed [he] is abusing it. That which we seek justly, because his [property] is his so unjustly, [and] another in using it unjustly acquires nothing of another's [property] if I am able [to stop] the unjust [acts]. But if he can in no way expel him, one must have recourse to the aid of a superior, so that he may provide those [remedies] which are of force and right. But if he or someone else impedes [him] so that he cannot repel [him] immediately, if he is able, otherwise he should have recourse to the superior, as above. However, it must be seen what "immediately" <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss> is, and what time [it involves]. Time, however, is not defined, but [is determined] by the immunity of both the mind and the thing, concerning which, although these things have been treated above, namely fifteen days—[concerning] which, since he is not present for the moment, it must be seen whether the disseised person was present or absent at the time of the disseisin, or he himself, or [his] dogs, or his equipment, or his household, or while he was absent, someone else entered into his empty possession. In the way, I say, [as to] the body, although not the mind. If, however, he was present at the time of the disseisin and chose this, so that he could not eject him immediately, [he is] facetiously [acting] as a disseisor. In this he chooses the disseisin itself, because if he wishes to pursue [it], having abandoned that way, [and] requests an addition, he will not be able to return to resist by his own authority in prejudice of the superior, to whom the cognizance has already devolved. But if he has not chosen such a way, it is estimated [to be] on the same day, or as much further with due grace, on the same day as he ought on the first day. But if, on the first day, he could not because of force, he can nevertheless resist in the estimation or in the interval of the law. He may also summon arms and the help of friends; but if he has waited for a long time, he will seem by this to have tolerated the injury, and this [applies] to the other part. It has been said, however, if the possessor is present or the family is present and is ejected: now it must be said if other things of his [are taken] and he himself were to enter through this [person] or through himself to hide, or what he might be able to repel from himself. But if he were absent

<column-break/>

when [he acts] with force, with veneration, or with fighting, or other opportunity, [one must] distinguish the place and the distance of time. [One must consider] diligence or negligence, according to whether the disseised person was in the same county or another, with law or elsewhere, provided that he is in the kingdom, not far or further, let it be distinguished. [One must consider] when he could have known that the disseisin was done, and at what time he knew it. From which case, upon finding [the facts], it is necessary [to determine] whence the reasonable days are [calculated], where [they are] allotted to him by his own authorities, and [the] reasonable [number of] days in which this may be done, as is aforesaid further, and then it is seen as a disseisin which he makes from then on <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss>; with the mind, [it is] to be done from then on. Since after the act he could have [sent] a messenger in that manner, if [he were] outside the kingdom by simple impetration [e.g., travel] to Saint James [of Compostela], or in the service of the lord king, perhaps in Gascony, he ought to have a delay of forty-five days, and one to be, and then [if] at sea. Similarly, if [he is] beyond the sea, [he may] come into the kingdom within forty-five days, as is plain, so that he may resume his strength. But if [he is] in the kingdom on a simple pilgrimage beyond Saint James, [he is entitled] to a delay of a year and a day, and then, as is plain. But if [he is] in a general passage to the Holy Land, a delay of two years and fifteen days will be given to him, then as aforesaid. And if someone else is within these terms [in relation] to the disseisor, if necessary the lord will warn him again in the same manner [that it is a] reasonable passage, which by another distant way the absence to be expected [would] then be valid, if he wishes to impetrate as before in the meantime, and because of devastation he will have perished. But all who have made longer delay than the restitution made <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss> seem to have given their rights to oblivion. Therefore, let him prudently [act] for himself by any right <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss>, while the disseisin is raging, [having] tolerated the injury of the present disseisor. For negligence in impetrating, sloth, or not expecting what has been impetrated [to be] done, by which he loses the natural possession of the truth, seems easy. And let [the case] of the vain disseisor begin here, such that if he cannot [act] then, [and] those who ought to be warned [are not], it seems from then on to be more than [enough]. So it is necessary that the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss> [be held] from then on; not that he wishes [to wait] for whatever time from here, [for] it seems he does not seek remedies for himself through the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>, as below. But if he had warned from then on, while the disseisin was raging, [and] having not recovered the passage [he] already suffered, that which he did, he [did] from then on in all-vance <note>a scribal or archaic term for "fully"</note> and I [tell] you to possess again, [and] still it is necessary [to seek] the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss> to recover the seisin, nor will it be infinite that [he] can warn [others] through possession by which it operates, and the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss> itself. And if then he [the disseisor] himself, [having been] convened, is able to despoil [him], the act [is] not [provided] to the worker of the disseisor who suffered [the loss]. But if the possessor is negligent and [is] after the disseisin and negligent in pursuing, [and] has tolerated the injury, [he must] impetrate in order [for the matter] to proceed from the power of the response so that he may [proceed] more justly to the passage. And if by chance he reserves the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss> and uses his possession by forces, [he] is not presumed to usurp [it] justly, [for] when he seeks the spoliation after the usurpation of the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>, [he] is not [one] who may be the disseisor in the matter. But if he who began [his] natural possession justly and through negligence or a divine way, yet [it seems] even if there is no day here [to] wish to [return] the way, as it is never said in the mind to seek [it] above. But if [he does] not [wish] to return to the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>, which works for him first, he will not be able to impetrate the royal [remedy] thereafter, but [must] invoke the aid of the law, which in the law of justice [is] the law in which anyone will opt for him. Item esto quod possessor ab disseisitore fecerit statim et eodem die quo disseisitus fuit spoliatum. ad alium transferat rem: queritur an possit ille ad quem res translata est incontinenti eia auctore domino disseisitore sicut ipse primus principalis disseisitor: et videtur quod sic. Dum semper sit retenta civilem possessionem quousque naturalem amiserit. Eodem modo si passim non disseisitus velit agere ipsum uti recuperabit. quia ubi fecit ei disseisinam principalis. primus disseisitor abstulit ei naturalem possessionem. secundus autem et res quietas simul ab alio abstulit et utrumque amiserit. et naturaliter et civiliter videtur contra sic alio respondere. Si enim unus primus tenetur ex disseisina tam ad penam et ius ad restitutionem quod non est in re. et secundus ad sedem ut tenet adhuc rem ad penam quia ad restitutionem. ad penam quia abstulit civilem possessionem ad restitutionem quia habet rem que debet restitui. Sed quid si primus post disseisinam per longum intervallum transtulerit ad alium inperitum. et ubi primus principalis disseisitor non tenet ad penam per inuriam tunc ad quem res spiritualis translata sunt an ad restitutionem secundum virtutem assise ut infra dicetur. Item esto quod primus disseisitor post disseisinam suam sine ab alio disseisitus fuerit utrique dominus si voluerit ulciscit disseisinam in continenti eiceat eum post intervallum per pacem videtur. Et eodem modo si per assisam ubi agere poterit usus vana age usque ad iusticiarium presentem. si autem ad tempus dissimulaverit poterit ille primus disseisitor in suam disseisinam revertere si agere velit passim possessionem ab invicem motu propria sicut et impeditus laboribus et plus de se si fecerit aliquo quo ille secundus in possessione se querit de recenti perrexit. an videtur de iure se intruisse videtur. quod sic minus quid dicitur sicut si ad aliud tempus non impune nec debet se ingerere ex officio suo si non potuerit disseisire quod si fecerit cadit in assisam. si videtur de vi et sine iusticia et violentia per regem iusticiarium ut in imposita vi autem in imposita de no inmittat ad alium inestimat ne ineat in assisam ne si aliquis alius disseisitus iniuste redisseisitus ad hoc invadat ut disseisitionem suam inmanem trahat si vi eum disseisia que iusta est amoverit tunc disseisitoris in impositam sustineat cadit in assisam. si alius qui venit ut iuste possidentem per vim deiciat ai possidens in possessione vi plie agat et se defendat. et vi eum inuasoris in impositam sustineat. cadit omnino in assisam. Dictum est supra quomodo disseisitus poterit disseisitorem suum incontinenti reicere in primis ubi qui vim detinuit civilem possessionem. sive aliter dicendum est quod recurritur ad superius auxilium ai utrumque amiserit possessionem naturalem videlicet et civilem. Cum igitur disseisitus ita negligens fuit in hac parte quod noluit vel non posset disseisitorem suum reicere de tenencia propria sua et ei per negligeniam. as no dis. multas vigilias et cogitacionem in iuvencia recuperande possessionis quia cum disseisitus iniuste amiserit sicut in do uero per summam omnium coin abis magis iuris sollempnitate qui propter negotium eminet loci a' uo solum hie vi assisam in rebus corporalibus sive in iuribus sicut iuribus et parit ad tenentia sicut de iure pascendi fodiendi nisi sic iustius appetit. Est autem ista recognitio sive assisa ex pluribus iunctis in lapis ut infra de restitutione dampnorum. Et si plures persequitur cuiusque disseisitorum pro sua tam quod se fecit. persequi enim ad penam et inuriam persequitur et cui quo ad restitutionem. Item videtur et propter actoris persequi et qui omnes pro quindium ad hoc agunt duos pro ut plures eodem tempore res ad ipsos pervenit per unam disseisinam vel post disseisinam per translationem statim ut postquam persequitur in quindium vnus pro quindium ad penam si fatur in inuriam etiam pro quindium ad restitutionem ai iam detineat. quare nulla sunt alia poterit respondere per se quod disseisitor non sit quid ipse aliter licet tenent ad penam. nec eam detinet licet possit restituere: nullam inuriam fecit. Convictus est vtrique pro in una tunc deinde peccat passim a uno alio. persequitur vbi plures per quindium ad penam et plures quindium ai ad restitutionem secundum quod res in plures manus devenerit post disseisinam vel secundum quod in plura capita ipsa disseisina divisa fuit et partita. Adquiritur vero passim ipsam non solum in re spoliata corporali: verum etiam in fructus medio tempore percepti. Item non solum ipsa res. scilicet in ipsa re per rames. sed non solum ipsa res. scilicet in libras et per lucris evanuerit. de quibus mico facta est in phap. Item quia ad omnis non pervenit vi querela quindium ius inpossessione fuerit videndus est quis au oportet remedium passim ad quem pertineat querela an si detineretur res ad quod non pertineat. et sciendum quod ad eum ad eosque la quod nomine suo pro tenuerit et in alieno. Sive adulti sine in fodo. scilicet non ad terminum annorum licet ad vitam et medium. Et quavis sunt tales masculi vel femina. maiores vel minores. ubi vel unus in suo casu et tunc per se tanta per sine per procuratorem vel familiam vel per se ipsum vel per alios quos ait qui suo nomine fuerit in fassi. ai per tales possideret. et ille possidet et nomine possidetur.

...with forces and right, [the] law does not aid him in his right, because if he could, he would not, and if he would, he could not. In the same way it answers him unless he has a just and sufficient impediment. Item, let it be that the possessor, immediately and on the same day on which he was disseised, has despoiled [the property] and transfers the thing to another: it is questioned whether he to whom the thing was transferred may [act] <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss>, with the lord disseisor as author, just as the first principal disseisor himself: and it seems that he may. Provided that the civil possession is always retained until he has lost the natural [possession]. In the same way, if he is not disseised, [and] wishes to act, he will recover it himself. Because where he made the disseisin to him, the first disseisor took away his natural possession. The second, however, and the quiet things [he] took away from another at the same time, and both [he] lost, both naturally and civilly, it seems [to] answer against him thus. For if one, the first, is held by reason of disseisin, as much for the penalty as [for] the right of restitution, which is not in the thing, and the second [is held] to the seat [of the court] as he still holds the thing, for the penalty [and] for the restitution; for the penalty because he took away the civil possession, [and] for the restitution because he has the thing which ought to be restored. But what if the first, after the disseisin, through a long interval has transferred [it] to another ignorant [person], and where the first principal disseisor is not held to the penalty by the injury, then [concerning] him to whom the spiritual things were transferred, whether [he is held] to restitution according to the virtue of the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>, as will be said below. Item, let it be that the first disseisor, after his disseisin, has been disseised by another: [to] both, the lord, if he wishes, avenges the disseisin <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss>, [he] may eject him after the interval by peace, it seems. And in the same way, if [he acts] through the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>, where he will be able to act, he uses a vain [process] until [he reaches] the present justice. **XXIII.**
But generally, in any *Hectic* [fever], the earwax is dry. Distillations are sharp and salty. Sweats [occur] on almost every night. Feces are generally dry, in some [cases] even liquid.

**XXIV.**
A changed quality is observed either in a part or in the whole.

**XXV.**
Thus, in a part, one encounters dry lippitude <note>inflammation of the eyelids</note> of the eyes (such as [that of] those who have completed a long journey in the sun and dust), concave eyes, collapsed temples, sharp nostrils, rigid ears and eyebrows. The vivid color of the face has perished; finally, the face is *Hippocratic* <note>a pinched, sunken, and pale facial expression indicative of impending death</note>.

**XXVI.**
In the whole, however, [there is] dryness and squalor, so that one appears as if a skeleton. For although digestion is poorly performed and the nourishment is depraved, cachexia <note>general physical wasting</note> does not occur, because it is consumed by the heat and dryness of the limbs: with apologies to Celsus, who seems to have listed cachexia among the species of Hectic. Heat is more distinct after food.

**XXVII.**
But if the Hectic [fever] is joined with a putrid [fever], it will have the signs of the putrid [fever] attached.

**XXVIII.**
To recognize an incipient Hectic [fever] is difficult, to cure one established is arduous, to know [one at its end] is easy. *Marasmodes* is immedicable, since the fibrous substance of the part cannot be restored.

Cooling is prompt but dangerous. Moistening, on the contrary, is safe but slow.

### XXXI.
Cooling and moistening agents are taken from those applied externally, from actions to be taken, and from those things which are consumed in any way. Of the first class are air, baths, <term>epithemata</term> <gloss>medicinal liquids applied with cloths</gloss>, and other topicals.

### XXXII.
If the air is not cold [and] moist, it should be prepared as such by art. Let the floor be sprinkled with cold water; let willow leaves, vine [leaves], flowers of roses, violets, and water lilies be strewn on the ground. But if it is too cold, as in winter, it ought to be heated.

### XXXIII.
A bath of sweet water was in great use among the Ancients and utilized with the utmost diligence. There are those who boil herbs in the bath water, namely violets, mallows, lettuces, calves' feet, and lambs' heads until the bones are bared of flesh. Sweat should not be excited in any way. The body should be gently cleansed from a rose or water-lily bath; immersion in cold water is also praised.

segura de lisonjas,
mis juveniles años
Amor no los malogra.
Pero necio discurso,
que mi exercicio estorvas,
en él no me diviertas
en cosa que no importa.
Quiero entregar la caña
al viento, y à la boca,
del pezecillo el cebo:
pero al agua se arrojan
dos hombres de una Nave,
antes que el Mar la sorba,
que sobre el agua viene,
y en un escollo aborda.
Las olas và escarbando,
y y su orgullo, y popa
casi la desvanece,
agua un costado toma,
Hundiôse, y dexô al viento
la gavia, que la escoja,
para morada suya,
que un loco en gavias mora.
*Dentr.* Socorro, que me ahogo.
*Tisb.* Un hombre à otro aguarda,
que dice que se ahoga,
gallarda cortesia,
en los ombros le toma:
Anchises le hace Eneas,
si el Mar estâ hecho Troya.
Ya nadando las aguas
con valentia corta,
y en la playa no veo
quien le ampare, y socorra.
Darè voces. Tirseo,
Anfriso, Alfredo, olas;
pescadores me miran,
plegue â Dios que oigan.
Mas milagrosamente
ya tierra los dos toman,
sin aliento el que nada,
con vida el que le estorva.

->*Saca en brazos Catalinon à Don Juan.*<-

*Catal.* Valgame la Cananea,
y qué salado estâ el Mar,
aqui puede bien nadar
el que salvarse desea.
Que allâ dentro es desatino,
donde la muger se fragua,
donde Dios juntô tanta agua,
no juntâra tanto vino?
Ha señor, elado estâ,
señor, si acaso estâ muerto?

<column-break/>

Del Mar fuê este desconcierto,
y mio este desvario.
Mal aya aquel que primero
pinos en la Mar sembrò,
y que sus rumbos midiô
con quebradizo madero.
Maldito sea Jason,
y Tifis maldito sea;
muerto estâ, no ay quien lo crea,
misero Catalinon:
què he de hacer?
*Tisb.* Hombre, què tienes
en desventuras iguales?
*Catal.* Pescadora, muchos males,
y falta de muchos bienes.
Veo por librarme â mì,
sin vida à mi señor; mira
si es verdad. *Tisb.* No, que aun respira;
ve â llamar los Pescadores,
que en aquella choza estân.
*Cat.* Y si les llamo vendrân?
*Tisb.* Vendrân por esto, no lo ignores:
quien es este Caballero?
*Cat.* Es hijo de aquel señor
del Camârero Mayor
del Rey, por quien ser espero
antes de seis dias Conde
en Sevilla, donde vâ,
y donde su Alteza estâ,
si al amistad corresponde.
*Tisb.* Como se llama? *Cat.* Don Juan
Tenorio. *Tisb.* Llama mi gente.
*Cat.* Ya voi. *vase.*

->*Coge en el regazo Tisbea à D. Juan.*<-

*Tisb.* Mancebo excelente,
gallardo, noble, y galan,
volved en vos, Caballero.
*Juan.* Donde estoi? *Tisb.* Ya podeis vêr,
en brazos de una muger.
*Juan.* Vivo en vos, si en el Mar muero:
y perdî todo el recelo
que me pudiera anegar,
pues del Infierno del Mar
salgo á vuestro claro cielo.
Un espantoso uracán
diò con mi nave al travês,
para arrojarme â essos pies,
que abrigo, y puerto me dân.
*Tisb.* Muy grande aliento teneis
para venir soñoliento,
y mas de tanto tormento,
mucho tormento ofreceis.
Pero si es tormento el Mar,

<header>The Trickster of Seville.</header>

secure from flattery,
my youthful years
do not waste in Love.
But foolish speech,
you who hinder my work,
do not distract me
with things of no importance.
I want to deliver the rod
to the wind, and to the mouth
of the little fish, the bait:
but into the water two men
from a Ship are thrown,
before the Sea swallows it,
which comes over the water,
and strikes upon a reef.
It is scraping the waves,
and its pride, and stern
it almost vanishes,
water takes on one side,
It sank, and left to the wind
the top-sail, for it to choose
as its dwelling,
for a madman dwells in top-sails.
<note>From within: Help, I am drowning.</note>
<note>Tisbea: One man awaits another, who says he is drowning; gallant courtesy, he takes him on his shoulders: he makes Aeneas to his Anchises, if the Sea is made Troy. Now swimming the waters with bravery he cuts, and on the beach I do not see who might protect and help him. I will call out. Tirseo, Anfriso, Alfredo, waves; fishermen look at me, may it please God that they hear. But miraculously now both reach land, the one who swims breathless, with life the one who carries him.</note>

->*Catalinon carries Don Juan in his arms.*<-

*Catal.* May the Canaanite woman help me,
and how salty the Sea is,
here he can swim well
who wishes to save himself.
For in there it is madness,
where woman is forged,
where God joined so much water,
would He not join so much wine?
Ah sir, he is frozen,
sir, if perhaps he is dead?

<column-break/>

This misfortune was from the Sea,
and this delirium of mine.
Accursed be the one who first
planted pines in the Sea,
and who measured its courses
with brittle wood.
Cursed be Jason,
and cursed be Tiphys;
he is dead, there is no one who can believe it,
miserable Catalinon:
what am I to do?
*Tisb.* Man, what do you have
in equal misfortunes?
*Catal.* Fisherwoman, many evils,
and a lack of many goods.
I see, to save myself,
my master without life; look
if it is true. *Tisb.* No, for he still breathes;
go to call the Fishermen,
who are in that hut.
*Cat.* And if I call them will they come?
*Tisb.* They will come for this, do not ignore it:
who is this Gentleman?
*Cat.* He is the son of that lord
the High Chamberlain
of the King, for whom I hope to be
before six days a Count
in Seville, where he is going,
and where his Highness is,
if he corresponds to the friendship.
*Tisb.* What is his name? *Cat.* Don Juan
Tenorio. *Tisb.* Call my people.
*Cat.* I am going. *He leaves.*

->*Tisbea takes D. Juan into her lap.*<-

*Tisb.* Excellent young man,
gallant, noble, and dashing,
return to your senses, Gentleman.
*Juan.* Where am I? *Tisb.* You can see now,
in the arms of a woman.
*Juan.* I live in you, if I die in the Sea:
and I lost all the fear
that could have drowned me,
since from the Hell of the Sea
I emerge to your clear sky.
A frightful hurricane
dashed my ship,
to throw me at those feet,
which give me shelter and port.
*Tisb.* You have great breath
to arrive sleepy,
and more than so much torment,
much torment you offer.
But if the Sea is torment,

son sus ondas crueles,
fuerza de los cordeles
enlo que os hacen hablar:
sin duda, que haveis bebido
al Mar la oracion passada,
pues por ser agua salada
tan grande sal ha sido.
Mucho hablais quando no hablais,
quando muerto venis,
mucho parece sentis,
plega à Dios que no mintais.
Pareceis caballo Griego,
que el Mar à mis pies desagua,
pues venis formado de agua,
y estais preñado de fuego.
Si mojado abrasais,
estando enjuto, què harèis ?
Mucho fuego prometeis,
plega à Dios que no mintais.
Juan. A Dios, Zigala, pluguiera,
que en el agua me anegara,
para que cuerdo acabara,
y loco en vos no muriera:
que el Mar pudiera anegarme
entre sus olas de plata,
que sus limites desata,
mas no pudiera abrasarme.
Gran parte del Sol mostrais,
pues que el Sol os dà licencia,
pues solo con la apariencia,
siendo de nieve abrasais.
Tisb. Por mas elado que estais,
tanto fuego en vos teneis,
que en este mio os ardeis,
plega à Dios que no mintais.

*Salen Catalinon, Anfriso, y Coridon, Pescadores.*

Cat. Ya vienen todos aqui.
Tisb. Y yà està tu dueño vivo.
Juan. Con tu presencia recibo,
el aliento que perdi,
Tisb. Què nos mandas? Tisb. Coridon,
Anfriso, amigos. Cor. Todos
buscamos por varios modos
esta dichosa ocasion.
Anfr. Di, què nos mandas, Tisbea,
que por labios de clavel,
no lo avràs mandado à aquel
que ido'atrarte desea
apenas, quando al momento,
sin cessar en llano, ò sierra,
sin que el Mar tale la tierra,
pisse el agua, el fuego, el viento.

<column-break/>

Tisb. O. què mal me parecían
estas lisonjas ayer,
y oy echo en ellas de vèr,
que sus labios no mentian!
Estando, amigos, pescando
sobre este peñasco, vì
hundirse una Nave allì,
y entre las ondas nadando
dos hombres, y compassiva
di voces, y nadie oyò,
y en tanta afliccion llegò
libre de la furia esquiva
del Mar, sin vida à la arena,
de este en los ombros cargado,
un Hidalgo, y anegado,
y embuelta en tan triste pena,
à llamaros embiè.
Anfr. Pues aqui todos estamos,
manda que tu gusto hagamos,
lo que pensado no fuè.
Tisb. Que à mi choza los llevemos
quiero, donde agradecidos
reparemos sus vestidos,
y allì los regalarèmos,
que mi Padre gusta mucho
de esta debida piedad.
Cat. Extremada es su beldad.
Juan. Escucha aparte. Cat. Ya escucho.
Juan. Si te pregunta quien soy,
di, que no sabes. Cat. A mi
quieres advertirme aqui
lo que he de hacer? Juan. Muerto soi,
por la hermosa Cazadora:
esta noche he de gozalla.
Cat. De què suerte? Juan. Ven, y calla.
Cor. Anfriso dentro de un hora,
que canten, y baylen.
Anfr. Vamos,
y esta noche nos hagamos
raxas, y palos tambien.
Juan. Muerto soi.
Tisb. Como, si andais?
Juan Ando en pena, como veis.
Tisb. Mucho hablais.
Juan. Mucho entendeis.
Tisb. Plega à Dios que no mintais.

*Vanse, y salen Don Gonzalo de Ulloa, y Don Alonso de Castilla.*

Rey. Como os ha sucedido en la embaxada,
Comendador Mayor?
Gonz. Hallè en Lisboa
al Rey D. Juan tu primo, previniendo
treinta Naves de Armada.

its waves are cruel,
the force of the ropes
is what makes you speak:
without a doubt, you have drunk
the last prayer to the Sea,
since for being salt water
so much salt there has been.
You speak much when you do not speak,
when you arrive dead,
you seem to feel much,
may it please God that you do not lie.
You look like a Greek horse,
which the Sea drains at my feet,
since you arrive formed of water,
and you are pregnant with fire.
If wet you burn,
being dry, what will you do?
You promise much fire,
may it please God that you do not lie.
*Juan.* Would to God, Zigala,
that I had drowned in the water,
so that I might end up sane,
and not die mad for you:
for the Sea could have drowned me
among its silver waves,
which unbind its limits,
but it could not burn me.
You show a great part of the Sun,
since the Sun gives you license,
for only with the appearance,
being of snow you burn.
*Tisb.* However frozen you are,
you have so much fire in you,
that you burn in this one of mine,
may it please God that you do not lie.

*Catalinon, Anfriso, and Coridon, Fishermen, exit.*

*Cat.* They are all coming here now.
*Tisb.* And your master is now alive.
*Juan.* With your presence I receive,
the breath that I lost.
*Tisb.* What do you command us? *Tisb.* Coridon,
Anfriso, friends. *Cor.* We all
seek by various means
this fortunate occasion.
*Anfr.* Say, what do you command us, Tisbea,
that by lips of carnation,
you will not have commanded it to that one
who desires to bring you
hardly anything, when at the moment,
without ceasing in plain, or mountain,
without the Sea cutting the land,
he treads the water, the fire, the wind.

<column-break/>

*Tisb.* Oh, how poorly I saw
these flatteries yesterday,
and today I see in them,
that his lips did not lie!
Being, friends, fishing
upon this cliff, I saw
a Ship sink there,
and among the waves swimming
two men, and compassionate
I called out, and no one heard,
and in such affliction arrived
free from the elusive fury
of the Sea, lifeless to the sand,
carried on the shoulders of this one,
a Nobleman, and drowned,
and wrapped in such sad pain,
I sent to call you.
*Anfr.* Well, here we all are,
command that we do your pleasure,
that which was not thought of.
*Tisb.* I want us to take them
to my hut, where grateful
we may repair their clothes,
and there we will treat them,
for my Father enjoys much
this due piety.
*Cat.* Her beauty is extreme.
*Juan.* Listen apart. *Cat.* I am listening now.
*Juan.* If she asks you who I am,
say, that you do not know. *Cat.* To me
you want to warn me here
what I am to do? *Juan.* I am dead,
for the beautiful Huntress:
tonight I must enjoy her.
*Cat.* In what way? *Juan.* Come, and be silent.
*Cor.* Anfriso, within an hour,
let them sing, and dance.
*Anfr.* Let us go,
and tonight let us make ourselves
shreds, and sticks too.
*Juan.* I am dead.
*Tisb.* How, if you are walking?
*Juan.* I walk in pain, as you see.
*Tisb.* You speak much.
*Juan.* You understand much.
*Tisb.* May it please God that you do not lie.

*They leave, and Don Gonzalo de Ulloa, and Don Alonso de Castilla exit.*

*King.* How has it gone for you on the embassy,
High Commander?
*Gonz.* I found in Lisbon
King D. Juan your cousin, preparing
thirty Ships of the Armada.

à Zeuta, ò Tanger pienſo que pretende

què es lo que concertaſteis?

à Serpa, y Mora, à Olivenza, y Toro,

*King.* And for where?
*Gonz.* For Goa he told me, but I understand,
that he prepares for another easier enterprise:
for Ceuta, or Tangier I think he intends
to besiege this Summer. *King.* May God help him,
and reward the Zeal of increasing his glory;
what is it that you have arranged?
*Gonz.* Lord, he asks
for Serpa, and Moura, for Olivenza, and Toro,
and for that he returns to Villa-verde,
to Almendral, to Mertola, and Herrera,
between Castile, and Portugal. *King.* Immediately
let the agreements be signed, Don Gonzalo:
But tell me first, how it has gone
on the journey, for you must be tired,
and exhausted as well.
*Gonz.* To serve you,
never, lord, am I tired.
*King.* Is Lisbon a good land?
*Gonz.* The greatest City in Spain:
and if you command that I say what I have seen,
of the exterior, and famous, in one point
in your presence I will put a portrait.
*King.* I will enjoy that, give me a chair.
*Gonz.* Lisbon is an Eighth Wonder.
From the bowels of Spain,
which are the lands of Cuenca,
is born the mighty Tagus,
which crosses half of Spain.
It enters the Ocean Sea,
on the salty shores
of this City, by the part
of the South; but before it loses
its course, and its clear name,
it makes a loop between two mountains,
where there are from all the World,
boats, ships, caravels.
There are Galleys, and frigates,
so many, that from the land
it seems a great City,
where Neptune reigns.
To the West side
they guard the Port two fortresses,
of Cascais, and São Julião,
the strongest of the land.
There is from this great City
little more than half a league
Belém, Convent of the Saint,
known for the stone.
And for the Lion of guard,
where the Kings, and Queens
Catholic, and Christian,

<column-break/>

have their perpetual houses.
Then this famous machine,
from Alcantara begins
to extend a great league
to the Convent of Odivelas <note>original: "Yobrega", likely referring to Odivelas or a monastery complex</note>.
In the middle is the beautiful Valley
crowned by three hills,
that Apelles would fall short,
when he wished to paint them.
Because looked at from afar
they seem pinecones of pearls,
that are hanging from the Sky,
in whose immense greatness
are seen ten Romes ciphered
in Convents, and in Churches,
in buildings, and streets,
in plots, and encomiendas,
in letters, and in weapons,
in the justice so straight,
and in a mercy,
that is honoring its shores.
And in that which I most praise
of this superb machine,
is, that from the same Castle,
at a distance of six leagues,
are seen sixty Places,
that the Sea reaches their doors,
one of which, is
the Convent of Odivelas,
in which I saw with my eyes
six hundred and thirty Cells,
and between Nuns, and Lay Sisters
they pass a thousand and two hundred.
It has from there to Lisbon,
at a very small distance,
one thousand one hundred and thirty Country Houses,
that in our Baetic Province
are called Cortijos, and all
with their Orchards, and Alamedas.
In the middle of the City
there is a superb Square,
that is called the Rocio,
large, beautiful, and well arranged,
that it must be one hundred years, and even more,
that the Sea bathed its sand,
and now from it to the Sea,
there are thirty thousand houses made,
that losing the Sea its course,
it extended to diverse parts.
It has a street that they call
Rua Nova, or New Street,
where the East is ciphered
in greatness, and riches:
so much,

མཆོད་པའ་ལྷ་མོའི་གང་། །རྒྱལ་ཆེན་བཞི་དང་ཐོད་པ་སྐམ་པོ་ལས། །གྲུབ་པའི་ཀ་བ་བརྒྱད་ཀྱི་ལེགས་བཏེགས་པའི། །ཐོད་པ་རློན་ཀ་གཞུ་རབ་ཏུ་བརྗིད། །
ཀླུ་ཆེན་བརྒྱད་ཀྱིས་གདུང་མས་ཕྱོགས་མཚམས་བྲེས། །དེ་ལ་མཛེས་པའི་རྡོ་རྒྱན་དུ་སྤུད། །གཟའ་ཆེན་བརྒྱད་ཀྱིས་པད་ཕུར་གཏང་བ་ལ། །རྒྱུ་སྐར་ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་
བརྒྱད་དྲལ་ལྕམ་བྱས། །བདུས་རྩི་ལྔ་ལས་གྲུབ་པའི་ཞལ་བ་ཅན། །དབུས་ཀྱི་ལྟེ་བར་ཕྱུར་ཕུར་མཐོ་བའི་རྩེར། །པདྨས་བཏེགས་པའི་ཙིཏྟ་ཏོག་གི་བརྒྱན། །སྒོ་
བཞིར་ཀ་བ་བཞི་བཞིས་བཏེགས་པ་ཡིས། །ཏ་བབས་བང་རིམ་བཞི་དང་ལྡན་པའི་སྟེང། །པདྨ་ཆོས་འཁོར་བཅུ་གསུམ་གདུགས་རི་དྭགས། །མགོ་སྙིང་ཏོག་
མཛེས་ཞིང་ཆེན་རྒྱལ་མཚན་དང་། །སག་པའི་ཕན་དང་སྐྲ་ཡི་རྔ་ཡབ་ཅན། །དབང་པོའི་མེ་ཏོག་སྲེལ་བའི་ཕྲེང་བ་གཡོ། །མདོར་ན་རྔམས་
བརྗིད་མཛེས་པའི་བརྒྱན་གྱི་སྤུད། །ཕྱི་རོལ་པད་ར་དུར་ཁྲོད་ཆེན་པོ་བརྒྱད། །རྡོ་རྗེར་བ་བསྐལ་པའི་མེ་དཔུང་འབར། །དབུས་ཀྱི་གྲུ་གསུམ་དམར་
<leaf-break/>
ཁམ་ནག་སྟུག་པོ་སྤུང་ཤིང་འཁྱིལ། །ཕྱག་གཡས་གསེར་གྱི་རྡོ་རྗེ་རྩེ་ལྔ་གདེངས། །གཡོན་པ་གནམ་ལྕགས་ཕུར་བུས་དགྲ་སྙིང་གཟིར། །གསང་གོས་
མཐིང་ཁ་ཟབ་བེར་གཡང་ལུག་སྟེང་། །གསེར་གྱི་པ་ཊ་ཧ་རིའི་སྣམ་སྦྱར་གསོལ། །སྙན་ཆ་དུང་ལོང་རིན་ཆེན་རུས་པས་སྤྲས། །མགོ་བོ་བརློན་པ་ལྔ་བཅུའི་
རྡོ་ཤལ་འཕྱང་། །ཞབས་གཉིས་བསགས་ལྷམ་གསོལ་ཞིང་གཡས་བསྐུམ་པས། །དམུ་སྟག་མི་ཟན་མགོ་བའི་སྟེང་ནས་མནན༔ གཡོན་པ་ཚང་སྟེང་
བརྐྱང་སྟེ་གར་གྱིས་འགྱིང་། །སྐུ་ལས་ཁྲོ་ཆུང་རྡོ་རྗེ་ཚ་ཚ་འཕྲོ། །རྩིབས་བཞིར་པདྨ་ཉི་མའི་གདན་སྟེང་དུ་ཤར་ནས་རིམས་བཞིན་དྲི་ཟ་འཆི་
བདག་ཀླུ། །གནོད་སྦྱིན་སྒོ་བཞིར་ཞིང་རྐྱང་གདན་སྟེང་ན། །གཙོ་བོའི་ཐུགས་ལས་ཧཱུཾ་ཡ་ཧྲིཿཧཱུཾ་དང་། །ཛཿཧཱུཾ་བཾ་ཧོཿའཕྲོས་པ་ཡོངས་གྱུར་
ལས། །ཤར་དུ་ཕྱག་རྡོར་ཞལ་གཅིག་ཕྱག་གཉིས་པ། །མཐིང་ནག་གཡས་པ་གསེར་གྱི་རྡོ་གསོར། །ལྷོ་རུ་གཤིན་རྗེ་ཞལ་གཅིག་ཕྱགཉིས་
<leaf-break/>
བཞུགས། །གཞལ་ཡས་ཁང་གི་ཐོག་མཚམས་བར་སྣང་ལ། །གཙོ་བོའི་དབུ་གཙུག་རིག་འཛིན་རྡོ་ཚོས། །མཐིང་ནག་རྡོ་རྗེ་དྲིལ་འཛིན་ཐོར་ཚུག་
ཅན། །རིན་ཆེན་རུས་རྒྱན་དར་གོས་དཀྱིལ་ཀྲུང་མཛད། །ཡུམ་ཆེན་རྡོ་རྗེ་རྣལ་འབྱོར་སྐུ་ལ་འཁྲིལ། །དེའི་ཕྱི་དུས་གསུམ་སངས་རྒྱས་པདྨ་འབྱུང་།
གསང་གོས་ཟབ་བེར་ཆོས་གོས་གཉེན་ཞུ་ཅན། །རྡོ་རྗེ་ཐོད་པ་ཁ་ཌཾ་རྩེ་གསུམ་བསྣམས། །དཀྱིལ་མཛད་ཅིང་སྲིད་གསུམ་ཟིལ་གྱིས་གནོན། །
དེའི་ལྷ་མི་མེ་ཏོག་རྒྱས་པའི་ཚུལ། །མཉམ་གཞག་ཨུཏྤལ་འཛིན་སྟེང་རལ་གྲི་མཚན། །དེའི་ཇའ་མཚོན་འཁོར་ཡུག་གསུམ་མཚམས་གྱིས། །
ནང་མར་པདྨ་ཉི་ཟླའི་གདན་སྟེང་དུ། །སྤྲུལ་པའི་རིག་འཛིན་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམ་པ་བརྒྱད། །གར་དུ་སློབ་དཔོན་ཆེན་པོ་ཧཱུཾ་ཀ་ར། །རྡོར་སེམས་གོས་དཀར་པོ་ཕུ་
ཐུང་ཅན། །ཕྱག་གཉིས་རྡོ་རྗེ་དྲིལ་བུ་ཐུགས་དཀར་བསྣོལ། །ལྷོ་རུ་སློབ་དཔོན་འཇམ་དཔལ་བཤེས་གཉེན་ནི། །གཤིན་རྗེའི་གསང་གོས་མཐིང་ནག་པུ

...all the offering goddesses.
From the four great kings and dry skulls,
the eight pillars of the structure are well-supported.
The beams of fresh skulls are very magnificent.
The eight great nagas form the beams across the directions and corners.
They are adorned with beautiful vajra-jewels.
The eight great planets form the lotus-daggers <term>pad-phur</term>,
and the twenty-eight constellations form the rafters and laths.
The floor is made of the five nectars.
At the center of the hub, on the tip of the high peak,
is the heart-jewel ornament supported by a lotus.
At the four doors, supported by four pillars each,
is the pediment <term>ta-bab</term> with four tiers.
On top is the lotus, the thirteen dharma-wheels, the umbrella, and the deer.
With a beautiful skull-top ornament, the great human-skin victory banner,
fringes of silk and whisks made of hair.
Garlands of sense-flowers wave.
In short, it is adorned with awesome, magnificent, and beautiful ornaments.
Outside is the lotus-fence and the eight great charnel grounds.
The vajra-tent blazes with the fire-masses of the aeon.
In the center is the triangular red...
<leaf-break/>
...dark brown, thick and gathered like a swirling mass.
The right hand raises a five-pointed golden vajra.
The left hand pierces the hearts of enemies with a meteoric iron dagger.
Over the secret blue robe and the heavy cloak, he wears a sheepskin.
He wears the golden monk's shawl <term>pati</term> and the yellow upper robe <term>hari</term>.
He is adorned with conch-shell earrings and precious bone ornaments.
A necklace <term>doshal</term> of fifty fresh human heads hangs down.
He wears boots on his two feet; with the right leg drawn in,
he tramples upon the head of a man-eating demon-tiger.
The left is extended over the void in a dancing posture.
Tiny wrathful vajra-sparks radiate from his body.
On the four spokes, upon the seats of lotuses and suns,
starting from the East are the Gandharva, the Lord of Death, the Naga,
and the Yaksha. At the four doors, on the seats of human skins,
from the heart of the principal deity, HUM, YA, HRIH, and HUM
and JAH HUM BAM HO are radiated.
From their total transformation:
In the East is Vajrapani with one face and two hands.
Dark blue, the right hand brandishes a golden vajra.
In the South is Yamantaka with one face and two hands...
<leaf-break/>
...they reside. At the roof-line of the celestial palace in the mid-air,
above the crown of the principal deity is the gathering of the Vajra Knowledge-Holders.
Dark blue, holding a vajra and bell, with a top-knot.
Adorned with precious bone ornaments and silk robes, sitting in the cross-legged posture.
The Great Mother Vajrayogini embraces his body.
Outside that is the Lotus-Born Buddha of the three times <note>Padmasambhava</note>.
Wearing the secret robe, the heavy cloak, the dharma robe, and the lotus hat.
Holding a vajra, a skull-cup, and a triple-pointed khatvanga.
Sitting in the cross-legged posture, he overwhelms the three worlds with his brilliance.
There, like a blooming flower of gods and men,
in the meditative posture, holding an utpala flower marked with a sword.
Within the three concentric rainbow circles:
On the inner one, upon seats of lotus, sun, and moon,
are the eight great emanated Knowledge-Holders.
In the East is the Great Master Humkara.
Vajrasattva attire, wearing a white robe with sleeves.
Two hands holding a vajra and bell crossed at the heart.
In the South is the Master Manjushrimitra.
Wearing the dark-blue secret robe of Yamantaka with sleeves...

ཀྲུང་མཛད། །ལྷོ་རུ་མཆོག་སྲེད་དཀར་པོ་ཐོད་རྔ་གཡས། །པད་ཕོར་རིན་ཆེན་རྒྱན་དང་དར་གིས་གོས། །ནུབ་ཏུ་ཉི་འོད་སེར་པོ་ཁ་ཊཾ་དང་། །སྡིག་འཛུབ་
ཉི་ཟེར་ཞག་འཛིན་སྟག་ཤམ་དཀྲིས། །རྒྱན་དྲུག་དར་དང་རིན་ཆེན་རྒྱན་གྱི་སྤུད། །བྱང་དུ་སེང་སྒྲག་མཐིང་ནག་ལྕགས་རྡོར་དང་། །སྡིག་འཛུབ་ཐོར་ཚུཊ

ཆེན་དང་ལྡན་མཆོག་སྦྱིན་གཡོན། །ལྷོ་ནུབ་པདྨ་རྒྱལ་དམར་དར་དམར་གོས། །ལྕགས་སྒྲོག་ཌ་རུ་མེ་ལོང་ཡིག་དྲུག་མཚན། །ནུབ་བྱང་ཤཱཀ་སེང་སྲེ་

ལྷོ་ནུབ་གཉགས་ཆེན་ཛྙཱ་ན་སྔགས་འཆང་ཆས། །བྲག་ལས་བབས་པའི་བདུད་རྩིས་ཐོད་པ་བསྐྱིལ། །ནུབ་བྱང་དཔལ་གྱི་སེང་གེ་རབ་བྱུང་ཆས། །
ཕན་ཞུ་གསོལ་ཞིང་དྲེགས་པའི་ལས་ལ་བཀོལ། །བྱང་ཤར་བཻ་རོ་རབ་བྱུང་མན་ཞུ་དམར། །དཔྲལ་བའི་དབུས་ན་གསལ་བའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་སྤྱན། །ཆོས
འཆད་གླེགས་བཾ་དྲག་སྔགས་དམོད་པ་འགྲུབ། །གཞན་ཡང་ལྷུན་གྲུབ་ཕྱག་རྒྱ་ཆེ་ལ་དབང་། །རྣམ་པར་སྨིན་སོགས་རིག་འཛིན་གྲངས་མེད་དང་། །
འོག་ཏུ་དཔའ་བོ་མཁའ་འགྲོ་ཆོས་སྐྱོངས་ཚོགས། །སྤྲིན་གྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྟ་བུར་འཁྲིགས་པར་གྱུར།། O ༒ །ལྔ་པ་བྱིན་རླབས་དབང་བསྐུར་བྱ་བ་ནི། ཧཱུཾ་ཐཾད་
སྐུ་གསུང་ཐུགས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལྡན། །དབང་ཆེན་དབང་བསྐུར་མཐུ་རྩལ་བྱིན་གྱིས་རློབས། །ཕྱག་རྒྱ་བཞི་ལྡན་ཡེ་ནས་གྲུབ་པའི་ངང་། །ཐམས་ཅད་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེཾས

འཁོར་བཅས་ཏིང་འཛིན་ཆོ་འཕྲུལ་གྱི། །རོལ་པ་མ་འདྲེས་ཕྱག་རྒྱའི་མཆོད་པ་འབུལ། །མ་ཧཱ་མུ་ཏྲ་པཱུ་ཙ་ཧོཿ བཅུ་པ་མུ་ཐོ་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་མཆོད་པ་ནི། ཧཱུཾ་ཡེ་ཤེས་གླུ་བྲོ་དོན་གྱི་
བརྡའ་མཚོན་ནས། །དགའ་བ་བཅུ་དྲུག་གླུ་དབྱངས་བྲོ་དང་གར། །ཡང་དག་དོན་རྟོགས་རང་བྱུང་རང་ལ་མཆོད། །རྟོགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་རང་གནས་བསྟན་དུ་གསོལ། །
མ་ཧཱ་ཛྙཱ་ན་ཏེ་ན་ཧཱུཾ། ཏེ་ན་ཏེ་ཏེ་ཧཱུཾ། བཅུ་གཅིག་པ་ཕྱིའི་ཉེ་བར་མཁོ་བའི་མཆོད་པ་ནི།། ཧཱུཾ་ཏིང་འཛིན་ཆོ་འཕྲུལ་ཡེ་ཤེས་རོལ་པ་ལས། །ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག

...white in color with a red radiance.
On the head, he wears a beautiful lotus-hat <term>pasha</term>.
He wears the silken dharma robes in the attire of a Nirmanakaya <gloss>Emanation Body</gloss>.
The two legs are in the cross-legged posture.
In the middle of the surrounding circle, upon lotuses, suns, and moons:
In the East is Padmasambhava, dark blue, hiding the six ornaments.
With five points, the scorpion-gesture, embracing the consort, he sits in the cross-legged posture.
In the South is Loden Chokse, white, holding a skull-drum in the right.
He wears a lotus-hat, precious ornaments, and silk robes.
In the West is Nyima Ozer, yellow, holding a khatvanga and
the scorpion-gesture, catching the sun's rays with a lasso, wearing a tiger-skin skirt.
Adorned with the six ornaments, silk, and precious jewels.
In the North is Senge Dradrok, dark blue, holding an iron vajra and
the scorpion-gesture, his top-knot bound with silk, standing in a wide-striding posture.
He wears a lion-skin upper garment and a tiger-skin skirt.
In the Southeast is Pema Sambhava in the attire of a monk.
Holding a skull-cup with a jewel, the left hand is in the supreme-generosity gesture.
In the Southwest is Pema Gyalpo, red, wearing red silk.
Holding a chain, a damaru drum, a mirror, and marked with the six syllables.
In the Northwest is Shakya Senge...
<leaf-break/>
In the Southeast is Drogmi with white robes, a top-knot, and so forth.
The mantra-holder raises a vajra in his right hand,
subjugating the mamo spirits as servants, and the left hand rests on the seat.
In the Southwest is Nyagchen Jnana in the attire of a mantra-holder.
He collects nectar falling from a rock into a skull-cup.
In the Northwest is Palgyi Senge in the attire of a renunciant.
Wearing a lotus-hat, he employs the arrogant spirits in activities.
In the Northeast is Vairotsana as a renunciant with a red lotus-hat.
In the center of his forehead is the clear eye of wisdom.
Through teaching the Dharma and volumes of scripture, the fierce mantra-curses are accomplished.
Furthermore, masters of the spontaneously accomplished Great Seal <term>Mahamudra</term>,
countless Knowledge-Holders of "Ripening" and so forth,
and below, the hosts of Heroes <term>Dakas</term>, Sky-Goers <term>Dakinis</term>, and Dharma Protectors,
gather like a mass of clouds. OM. Fifth, the blessing and empowerment:
HUM. All are endowed with Body, Speech, Mind, and Wisdom.
Bestow the empowerment of the Great Power and bless us with strength and skill.
The state of primordial accomplishment endowed with the four mudras,
everything is the heart of enlightenment...
<leaf-break/>
...with the entourage, through the magical display of meditative absorption.
I offer the unmixed display of the mudra-offering.
MAHA MUDRA PUJA HO. Tenth, the wisdom-offering of Mutho:
HUM. Representing the symbolic meaning of the wisdom-song and dance,
the sixteen joys, songs, melodies, and dances.
Realizing the perfect meaning, I offer the self-arisen to itself.
I pray that you show the wisdom of realization in its own place.
MAHA JNANA TENA HUM. TENA TETE HUM. Eleventh, the offering of outer necessities:
HUM. From the display of the wisdom of the magical meditative absorption,
the offering clouds of the perfected six paramitas.
Firmly established in the manner of an illusion in the realm of space,
I offer to the deity of the meaning of self-arisen awareness.
OM VAJRA AHARA AHARA.
PUSHPE. DHUPE. ALOKE. GHANDHE. NEVITE. SHAPTA PUJA HO. Twelfth, offering the inner sensual qualities:
HUM. The supreme bliss of the Secret Mother.
Forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and phenomena.
Through the unceasing self-arisen goddesses of the sensual qualities,
I offer the supreme bliss as the ornament of the mind.
PANCHA KARMA GUNA PUJA HO. Thirteenth, the secret...

Koomt niet als met befcheyt ontrent het tweede bed,
Een jaer is voor de rouw, dat is een oude wet.
Ghy mooght na defen tijt (of immers na de keuren,
Die yder lantfchap heeft als eygen om te treuren)
Gaen ftrecken u gebet, op dat de wijfe God
Mach ftieren u gemoet in dit onfeker lot.
Doch fchoon ghy wort verfocht, gevleyt, en aengebeden,
Om voor de tweedemael in echten ftaet te treden,
En ftelt u geenfins aen gelijck een vryfter doet,
Die met een ydel breyn haer eerfte liefde broet:
En houd geen mal gevry, en pleeght geen minneftreken,
En laet niet door de ftadt van uwen handel fpreken;
Weeft ftil in u bedrijf, en deckt u ganfch beleyt
Tot dat het in de kerck voor yder wort gefeyt.
Ghy moet in dit beflagh ten naeueften overleggen,
En wat 'er is te doen, en wat 'er is te feggen,
Maeckt dat u niet een menfch in woorden achterhaelt,
't Is beter dat de voet, als dat de tonge dwaelt.
En laet geen nieuwen vrient aen uwen fin behagen,
Of pleeght al voren raet, oock met de naefte magen
Van uwen eerften man; (b) dat is een foete vont
Die nieuwe banden maeckt, en ftijft het oude bond:
Doet niet in dit geval door eygen-finnigheden,
Hout vrientfchap daerje plaecht, dat eyffchen goede feden:
Al benje van den man en fijnen wil gevrijt,
Weet datje niettemin noch aen de vrienden fijt.
Men hoort den ouden tijt van jonge weuwen klagen,
Om datfe veel beftaen, en efter weynigh vragen,
Of, fchoon fy plegen raet, ten is maer enckel fchijn,
Sy willen evenwel niet afgeraden fijn.
Hoe dwalen overal, hoe dolen jonge vrouwen,
Die voor de tweedemael haer fnellen om te trouwen,
't Is wonder wat men hoort, en wat men dickmael fiet,
Wanneer de krevel-fucht haer in de leden fchiet,
Dees trout een vreemden haen om dat hy weet te fingen,
En geen 'een lichte-voet om dat hy weet te fpringen,
De derd' een jongen wulp van onbefuyden aert,
Of om een kroefe kop, of om een krullen baert.
Ghy faet met alle forgh op uwe faecken letten,
Eer fich in eenigh deel u finnen neder fetten;
,,Noyt wort 'er goet beleyt in eenigh ding gepleeght,
,,Als daer men eerft het ftuck met gave finnen weeght.
Indienje vryers hebt die aen het herte raecken,
En datje wort verfocht u keus te willen maecken,
Soo wacht u door het vleys te worden afgeleyt,
Maer wickt in u gemoet wat u de reden feyt.
En kieft geen jongen laf in weelden uytgelaten,
Die voor een lanterfant gaet proncken achter ftraten,
En kieft geen vremdeling, die moytjens opgefet
Loert om den vetten ael te locken in het net:
En foo de friffe jeught van uwe groene jaren
Is tot de vrucht bequaem, en luftigh om te baren,
Soo kieft noch grijfen baert noch tandeloofen mont,
Al wort fijn goet begroot op menigh duyfent pont.
En kieft u boven al, indienje fijt te raden,
En kieft u geenen man met kinders overladen;

En, fooje niet en wilt verfmachten in verdriet,
En kieft in dit geval, en kieft u jonger niet.
Wat van het eerfte rot, een deel van defe gaften
En heeft geen ander wit als in het goet te taften,
Geen ander oogh-gemerck, als wel en luftigh fijn,
En flechs tot uwen koft te fitten in den wijn:
En als foodanigh volck ontrent de vremde menfchen
Heeft in het fpel gebracht al wat de luften wenfchen,
Soo komt het treurigh t'huys, en fit gelijck een block,
Een ander heeft de vreught, en ghy alleen de wrock:
Wat mooghje jonge vrou, wat mooghje doch verlangen?
De vreught van dieje wacht blijft aen de klopper hangen,
Wat geeft de leven had is buyten al gequijt,
Voor u en reft 'er niet als flechs alleen de gijt.
Nu tot het tweede deel, een ouden man te trouwen
Is enckel herten-leet voor alle jonge vrouwen,
Gelooft het, warte doet, of hoe de faecken gaen
Ghy fijt, in dit geval, ghy fijt 'er qualick aen:
Indienje lieve-kooft, een yder fal gelooven
Dat u bevenfde gunft fijn kaffe wil berooven;
Indienje deftigh fijt, foo roept de ganfche ftad
Dat ja u gulle jeught een jonger liever had:
Indienje liefde pleeght, ghy fult 'er al verkerven;
Want jonge lieden vreught doet oude lieden fterven,
Of fooje machtigh fijt te leven fonder man,
Wie is 't die aen het volck de monden ftoppen kan;
Dit maeckt dan over al een angftigh mis-vertrouwen,
Een pijn-banck voor den man, een helle voor de vrou.
wen;
Ach! 't is een vinnigh menfch, en hart gelijck een
De dot en levend vleys wil binden over een.
Koomt tot het derde ftuck, veel kinders fonder baren
Sijn niet als enckel leet ontrent de friffe jaren,
En Stief-moer is een woort dat al te vinnigh luyt,
Een jongen boven al ontrent een jonge bruyt: D
Men noemt ons feker lant, der op befette reden,
Noyt in den breeden Raet een man en wert geleden
Die lieve kinders had, foo veel hem dienen mocht,
En efter in het huys een tweede moeder brocht:
Een jongen, die een hont eens dapper wilde treffen,
Vermits hy voor het huys niet af en liet te keffen,
Roght juyft fijns vaders wijf, en, met dat hy het wift,
Soo riep hy tot het volck: het is niet al gemift.
Siet! wat een bitter leet, en wat een hatigh wefen,
Is in den harden naem van dit beroep te lefen:
Ghy, die een fteunfel foeckt voor uwen fwacken aert,
Trout daerje moeder wort, en eygen kinders baert.
Ten leften, jonge vrou, wat fijnder fware klachten:
Wat fijnder over al, wat fijnder droeve nachten
Te vinden by het volck, alleen op defen gront
Om dat haer koetfe fcheef, en niet gelijck en ftont?
Die groen en luftigh als uwe dagen korten,
Die meynt, het ftaet hem vry in luften uyt te fforten.
En dat fijn friffe jeught, oock op den vollen dagh
Een fchoonder newens u, of jonger hebben magh.
Vriendinnen, om verdriet en alle twift te fchouwen,
O tracht met uws gelijck, en anders niet, te trouwen,
Of fooje niet en kont bereycken defe wet,
Ten minften houd den voet die elders is gefet;

Indienje veertigh telt, foo dienje niet te paren
Met een die niet en komt tot vijf-en-dertigh jaren;
En foo daer eenigh man de t'feftigh overleeft,
Hem dient geen jonge vrou die min als dertigh heeft.
Siet daer een rechte peyl, die, foo het mochte wefen,
Wel diende voor een wet te worden afgelefen:
Ghy, foeckt gelijck te fijn met uwen bed-gefel,
,,Twee offen niet gelijck en ploegen nimmer wel.
En laet hier u gemoet niet wilt en dertel fwieren,
Maer ftelt u voor een wit befetheyt van manieren;
En trout niet voor het oogh, maer kieft een fedigh
man,
Die met een foet beleyt u finnen buyten kan:
Is vry een groot behulp een man te mogen krygen
Die laegh in fijnen geet, om hooge weet te ftygen,
Die met een ftille fiel, en met een reyn gemoet
Als uyt den hemel fiet wat ftot en aerde doet.
Die kan u in geluck van alle waen bevryden,
Defal u gulle pracht in weelde leeren myden,
Die fal u fteunfel fijn, wanneer het qualick gaet,
En houden overal de rechte middel-maet.
Indien fije geneyght u tochten af te breken,
Die noch van ouden tijt in u wen boefem fteken,
Hy ful u wijfen aen hoe dat 'er dient gewracht,
En hoe het ydel breyn moet onder fijn gebracht:
Indienje raet begeert, oock in bekaeyde faecken,
Om weder recht te gaen, en uyt den neer te raecken,
Hy fal u leyder fijn, en brengen aen den dagh
Al wat u in den geeft ten goede dienen magh:
't korte, wat 'er is of dienftigh aen de leden,
Of mit voor u bedrijf, of noodigh in de feden,
Of heyflaem voor de fiel, oock in den laeften noot
Hy fal u fteunfel fijn tot in de bleecke doot.
En paff u nimmermeer de bruyt te laten maecken,
Of fooje kinders hebt) vereffent alle faecken;
Geeft hun dat reden is, aleer een tweede man
U gunfte tegenftaen of wederhouden kan,
Wary het tegendeel voor ongemacken ryfen
En over al de taet aen yder aen te wyfen,
Ick weet een jonge weeuw van alle man beklaeght
Die in haer leden felfs hier van noch teykens draeght;
Sy uyt een luchten fin met trou-fucht aengedreven,
Had een jong-gefel haer rechterhant gegeven
Als pant van haer gemoet, en doen het was te alemift.
Ontdeckte wat 'er fchuylt, en vordert goeden raet;
Waer toe hier groot misbaer? of fchoon de vrienden
kijven,
Deknoop is vaft geleyt, en moet geduerigh blijven;
Een neef des niettemin beweeght de jonge vrou,
Dat fy haer eenigh kint wat naerder doen fou;
Devoorflagh wort gevolght en in der haeft befchreven,
Verleden na den eych, en aen den vooght gegeven
Ten ifliften dat men kan, daer tout de bly bruyt,
Maer fiet! cer langen tijt de faecken komen uyt:
Stax wort het gefchil hier over aengefteken,
De man wil door het rech den ganfchen handel breken,
Hy noemt 'et flim beleyt, als fonder hem gedaen,
Hy noemt 'et quaet bedrogh dat niet en kan beftaen;
De vooght drijft even feer, dat ja verloofde vrouwen
Sijn machtigh hares goets tot aen het wettigh trouwen;
Daer, na den rechter toe, het huys leyt over hoop,
Het wijf fit in den druck, de man is op de loop:
Het ftuck wort onder dies door al het lant geweten,
Noch en is de wrock op heden niet gefleten,

<margin>g Geen cenft hee eft Conftitutio quam refert & laudat Cyprian Traff. de fponfalibus, l. 9. num. 12.</margin>

<column-break/>

Maer waft geduerigh aen; en waerom meer gefeyt?
Een gants verloren huys alleen uyt quaet beleyt.
Vriendinnen, fedigh volck, wilt defe klippen myden,
En ter rechter ftont van alle laften vryden;
Doet oude fchulden af, maeckt alle flommer quijt,
U eefte dient te fijn gelijck een nieuwen tijt:
't Is dickmaels aengemerckt dat, naer het tweede paren,
En twift en huys-gefchil haer felder openbaren,
En vry al wranger fijn als in het eerfte bed
Daer eenigh jeughdigh paer te famen is gefet;
De reden is bekent, twee herten fonder bochten
Van eerften aen gevoeght en in der jeught gevlochten
Sijn onder een gepaert en over een geleyt
Gelijck men mande-werck van fwacke teenen breyt;
Maer alfer eenich volck te famen is gekomen,
Dat in een voorigh bed fijn floyen heeft genomen,
Wat is daer ongemacx, eer dat het eerfte krom
Kan buygen na den eyfch, en keeren anders om?
Ghy, die genegen fijt om noch eenmael te trouwen,
Leert, na de tijt vereyft, in nieuwe bochten vouwen;
Hier dient al meerder kunft, en vry al grooter kracht
Als die u fwacke jeught heeft aen den man gebracht:
Wilt voor een nutte les in dit beginfel leeren,
Hoe van den eerften man u finnen af te keeren,
Hoe in het tegendeel de tweede dient gekent,
En hoe u gants bedrijf naer hem te fijn gewent:
Veel op een vprigh man in defen ftaet te roemen,
Hem dan oock eere doen, en over al te noemen,
Is geenfins na den tijt, 't is beter datje viert
De Son, de nieuwe fon, die nu den hemel ciert.
Wat dient een eerfte man van u te fijn geprefen?
't En kan hem, daer hy is, doch geenfins dienftigh wefen;
En hy, die maer alleen nu dient te fijn bemint,
Wort over dit verhael ten hooghften ongeflint;
Hy beelt hem feker in, dat u ontijdigh prijfen
Hem pooght als metter hant fijn feylen aen te wijfen;
En, fchoon ghy niet te fcherp of niet te fchamper fijt,
Hy duyt 'et evenwel alleen tot enckel fpijt.
Veel dingen fijn gewoon ons foeter in te komen
Om datfe van het oogh alreede fijn genomen,
Maer 't is bekaey de luft die niemant bluffen kan,
Ghy, voeght u naer den tijt en eert nu defen man:
Eert hem die met u leeft, en laet den dooden ruften,
Dat niet in wefen is, en moet u niet geluften:
Naer dat u rechterhant her tweede trouwe gaf,
Soo dient het eerfte bont gelaten in het graf.
Doet hier gelijck de Bye, die mijt de dorre rofen,
En fet haer op de bloem die eerft begint te blofen;
Vriendinne, tot befluyt, ghy die den tweeden trout,
Siet datje 't in der daet oock metten tweeden hout.
't En is niet lofs genoeg al wort een wijf geprefen
Van tucht, en eerbaer root, of van een deftigh wefen,
Sy moet genoegfhaem fijn, en heulen met den man
Al eerf haer echten plicht ten vollen treffen kan.
'k En wil noch evenwel geen vrouwen gaende maken,
Om by haer tweeden vrient den eerften oyt te laken,
Neen, beter niet gefeyt: ghy, fpreckje goet of quaet,
't Is tegen u beroep, en buyten onfen raet;
'fen weduw heeft gelijck van haeren man te fpreken,
'en tot deffelfen lof by wijlen uyt te breken;
,,Maer alfe weder trout, en nieu gefelfchap krijgt,
,,Dan iffe wel bedacht, indienfe ftille fwijght.

controverfiam eft, & licet plurimae & magni momenti rationes pro poteftate fponfae
allegari poffint, praefes tamen Everard. pro fponfo contra alienationem refpondet.

<meta>This page continues the moral guidance for a widow, moving from the initial period of grief to the practical and ethical considerations of remarriage. It offers specific warnings about age gaps, step-children, and financial disputes.</meta>

### WIDOW

->Approach the second marriage bed only with discretion;<-
->A year is for mourning, that is an ancient law.<-
You may, after this time (or according to the customs
That every province has as its own for mourning)
Set forth your prayer, so that the wise God
May steer your mind in this uncertain fate.
Though you be sought, flattered, and adored
To enter into the wedded state for the second time,
Do not behave at all like a young maiden does,
Who broods over her first love with a vain brain:
Do not keep up a foolish courtship, or use lovers' tricks,
And do not let the city speak of your dealings;
Be quiet in your conduct, and cover your whole plan
Until it is announced to everyone in the church.
In this undertaking you must consider most closely,
Both what is to be done, and what is to be said,
Ensure that no person catches you in your words;
It is better that the foot wanders than the tongue.
And let no new friend please your fancy,
Without first taking counsel, even with the nearest kin
Of your first husband; <margin>b</margin> that is a sweet invention
Which makes new bonds, and strengthens the old tie:
Do not act in this case out of stubbornness,
Maintain friendship where you are accustomed; good manners require this:
Though you are freed from the man and his will,
Know that you are nevertheless still bound to the friends.
One hears the old times complain of young widows,
Because they undertake much, and yet ask little advice,
Or, though they seek counsel, it is but a mere appearance;
They do not wish to be discouraged anyway.
How young women everywhere wander and stray,
Who hasten to marry for the second time;
It is a wonder what one hears, and what one often sees,
When the <term>krevel-fucht</term> <gloss>restless desire</gloss> shoots into their limbs.
This one marries a strange rooster because he knows how to sing,
And another a light-foot because he knows how to jump,
The third a young wildling of reckless nature,
Either for a curly head, or for a curled beard.
You must look to your affairs with all care,
Before your senses settle in any part;
"Never was good management practiced in anything,
"Unless one first weighs the matter with sound senses.
If you have suitors who touch the heart,
And you are requested to make your choice,
Then beware of being led astray by the flesh,
But weigh in your mind what reason tells you.
And do not choose a lazy youth given to luxury,
Who struts behind the streets like a loafer,
And do not choose a stranger, who, finely dressed,
Lurks to lure the fat eel into the net:
And if the fresh youth of your green years
Is fit for fruit, and lusty to bear,
Then choose neither a gray beard nor a toothless mouth,
Though his wealth be valued at many thousand pounds.
And choose for yourself above all, if you are to be advised,
Do not choose for yourself a man overloaded with children;

<margin>a The mourning time prescribed for women today is a year, and this is not only because of the confusion of blood <note>referring to potential pregnancy from the deceased husband</note>, but out of reverence for the husband, since a woman is bound to complete the time of mourning even if she gives birth within the year. <note>original: Latin citations of legal codes by Godefredus and others</note></margin>

<margin>b A woman, if having lost her husband she fears falling into the snare of her weakness, if she wishes, let her marry in the Lord, provided that she defers the choice of a husband to her parents, lest her desire be seen as the author of it, if she claims the choice of marriage for herself. For she ought to seem sought after by the man, rather than she herself having sought the man. <note>original: Ambrose, Book on the Patriarch Abraham</note></margin>

<margin>c Of all this, lively and well-known examples could be given, if the time and place permitted.</margin>

<column-break/>

And, if you do not wish to pine away in sorrow,
Do not choose, in this case, do not choose one younger than you.
As for the first group, a portion of these guests
Have no other aim than to reach for your wealth,
No other goal but to be well and merry,
And merely to sit in the wine at your expense:
And when such people, among strangers,
Have brought into play all that their lusts desire,
They come home mournfully, and sit like a block;
Another has the joy, and you alone have the resentment:
What can you, young woman, what can you still long for?
The joy of the one you expect stays hanging on the door-knocker;
Whatever gave life to the skin is all gone;
For you nothing remains but only the greed.
Now to the second part: to marry an old man
Is mere heartache for all young women,
Believe it, whatever you do, or however things go,
You are, in this case, you are badly off:
If you show affection, everyone will believe
That your feigned favor wants to rob his chest;
If you are dignified, then the whole city cries
That indeed your generous youth would rather have a younger man:
If you practice love, you will spoil everything;
For the joy of young people makes old people die.
Or if you are able to live without a husband,
Who is it that can stop the mouths of the people?
This then creates an anxious mistrust everywhere,
A rack for the husband, a hell for the wife;
Alas! it is a fierce thing, and hard like a stone,
To want to bind dead and living flesh together.
Come to the third point: many children without bearing them yourself
Are nothing but pure sorrow around the fresh years;
And "Stepmother" is a word that sounds all too fierce,
Especially for a youth around a young bride: <margin>d</margin>
In a certain land, they say with established reason, <margin>e</margin>
Never was a man allowed in the Great Council
Who had dear children, as many as might serve him,
And yet brought a second mother into the house.
A boy, who once wanted to hit a dog bravely,
Because it would not stop barking in front of the house,
Hit exactly his father's wife, and, as soon as he knew it,
He cried out to the people: it was not a total miss.
See! what a bitter sorrow, and what a hateful being,
Is to be read in the hard name of this vocation:
You, who seek a support for your weak nature,
Marry where you will become a mother, and bear your own children.
Lastly, young woman, what heavy complaints there are:
What are found everywhere, what sad nights
Are to be found among people, only on this ground
Because their bed stood crooked, and not level?
He who is green and lusty like your shortened days,
Thinks he is free to pour himself out in pleasures,
And that his fresh youth, even in the full day,
May have a fairer or younger one beside you.
Friends, to avoid sorrow and all strife,
Oh, try to marry your equal, and nothing else,
Or if you cannot reach this law,
At least keep the pace that is set elsewhere;

<margin>d Regarding the stepmotherly hatred and the epithets of stepmothers, see Tiraqueau... although these are not always true; as appears from the laws where a stepmother bequeathed five pounds of gold to her stepson... and where a certain woman appointed her stepson as heir. <note>original: Latin legal references</note></margin>

<margin>e Annaeus Robertus records this concerning the Sybarites.</margin>

<margin>f See the Civil Conversation of Guazzo, book 3.</margin>

<column-break/>

If you count forty years, then you should not pair
With one who has not reached thirty-five years;
And if any man outlives sixty,
He should have no young wife who has less than thirty.
Behold there a right standard, which, if it could be,
Well deserved to be read out as a law:
You, seek to be equal with your bed-companion,
"Two unequal oxen never plow well."
And do not let your mind wander wild and wanton,
But set as your goal a composure of manners;
And do not marry for the eye, but choose a modest man,
Who can govern your senses with a sweet management:
It is truly a great help to be able to get a man
Who, low in his spirit, knows how to rise high,
Who with a quiet soul, and with a pure mind,
As if from heaven, sees what dust and earth do.
He can free you from all delusion in good fortune,
He will teach you to avoid your generous splendor in luxury,
He will be your support when things go badly,
And maintain the right middle path everywhere.
If you are inclined to break off your passions,
Which still stick in your bosom from old times,
He will show you how work should be done,
And how the vain brain must be brought under control:
If you desire counsel, even in troubled matters,
To go right again, and to get out of the slump,
He will be your leader, and bring to light
Whatever may serve you for the good in the spirit:
In short, whatever is either useful to the limbs,
Or fit for your conduct, or necessary in manners,
Or healthy for the soul, even in the final need,
He will be your support until pale death.
And never allow yourself to be made the bride,
(If you have children) before settling all matters;
Give them what is reasonable, before a second man
Can oppose or withhold your favor from them,
Lest the contrary should rise into troubles
And the deed be pointed out to everyone everywhere.
I know a young widow pitied by everyone
Who even in her own limbs still carries signs of this;
She, driven by a light mind and a desire to marry,
Had given a young fellow her right hand
As a pledge of her mind, and when it was all a mistake.
She discovered what was hidden, and sought good advice;
Why great outcry here? even though the friends scold,
The knot is tied fast, and must remain continuously;
A kinsman nevertheless persuaded the young woman,
That she should move her only child somewhat closer <note>meaning, to secure the child's inheritance before the marriage</note>;
The proposal was followed and described in haste,
Passed according to the requirement, and given to the guardian
In the cleverest way possible; then the happy bride marries,
But see! before long the matters come out:
Immediately the dispute was ignited over this,
The husband wants to break the whole transaction through the law,
He calls it a sly plan, as done without him,
He calls it a bad fraud that cannot stand;
The guardian insists just as much, that indeed betrothed women
Are masters of their property until the legal marriage;
Then, to the judge! the house lies in a heap,
The wife sits in distress, the man is on the run:
The matter meanwhile becomes known throughout the land,
Nor is the resentment settled even today,

<margin>g Not unlike this is the Constitution which Cyprianus refers to and praises... <note>original: Latin reference to betrothal contracts</note></margin>

<column-break/>

But grows continuously; and why say more?
A completely lost house solely from bad management.
Friends, modest people, seek to avoid these cliffs,
And free yourselves from all burdens at the right moment;
Pay off old debts, get rid of all clutter,
Your first marriage should be like a new time:
It is often noted that, after the second pairing,
Both strife and domestic dispute reveal themselves more quickly,
And are quite a bit more bitter than in the first bed
Where any youthful pair was set together;
The reason is known: two hearts without bends
Joined from the first and woven in youth
Are paired together and laid over each other
Just as one weaves basket-work from weak willow twigs;
But when some people have come together,
Who have taken their folds in a previous bed,
What trouble is there, before the first curve
Can bend to the requirement, and turn the other way?
You, who are inclined to marry once more,
Learn, as the time requires, to fold into new curves;
Here more art is needed, and quite a bit greater strength
Than that which brought your weak youth to the husband:
Take as a useful lesson in this beginning,
How to turn your senses away from the first husband,
How on the contrary the second should be acknowledged,
And how your whole conduct should be accustomed to him:
To boast much about a former husband in this state,
To do him honor then, and to name him everywhere,
Is not at all according to the time; it is better that you celebrate
The Sun, the new sun, that now adorns the heaven.
Why should a first husband be praised by you?
It can, where he is, be of no service to him;
And he, who alone should now be loved,
Is highly offended by this tale;
He imagines for certain, that your untimely praising
Tries as if by hand to point out his failings;
And, even if you are not too sharp or too mocking,
He nevertheless interprets it only as pure spite.
Many things are accustomed to seem sweeter to us
Because they have already been taken from the eye,
But it is a spoiled desire that no one can quench,
You, adapt to the time and honor this man now:
Honor him who lives with you, and let the dead rest,
That which is not in being must not please you:
After your right hand gave the second pledge,
The first bond should be left in the grave.
Do here like the Bee, which avoids the withered roses,
And sets herself on the flower that first begins to blush;
Friend, in conclusion, you who marry the second,
See that you also truly hold with the second.
It is not enough praise though a wife be commended
For discipline, and modest blushing, or for a dignified being,
She must be sufficient, and conspire with the man
Before her wedded duty can be fully met.
I do not wish, however, to incite any women,
To ever disparage the first by their second friend,
No, better not said: you, whether you speak good or evil,
It is against your calling, and outside our advice;
A widow has the right to speak of her husband,
And to break out in his praise at times;
"But if she marries again, and gets new company,
"Then she is well-advised, if she keeps silent.

<margin>h Whether a bride, without the knowledge and consultation of the groom, can alienate her goods is not entirely without controversy; and although many and weighty reasons can be alleged for the power of the bride, nevertheless President Everardus responds for the groom against the alienation. <note>original: Latin legal references regarding pre-marital property transfers</note></margin>

<summary>This page provides ethical and practical advice for widows considering remarriage, emphasizing the importance of a year of mourning and the selection of a compatible partner. It warns against the legal and emotional pitfalls of marrying too young or old, and the difficulties of managing step-children and pre-marital property disputes.</summary>
